abstract: Since the 2000s, U.S. public pension funds have actively shifted their risky investments away from public equities and toward alternative assets like private equity and hedge funds—some much more than others. We explore a range of possible explanations for these trends and argue that beliefs about the risk-adjusted return of alternatives have played a central role. Pension beliefs are shaped by investment consultants, peers, and experience in the 1990s. Other demand-side channels related to risk-seeking motives, spending needs, and fund governance have weaker empirical support. We also consider supply-side factors and agency interpretations of the data. (JEL G11, G23, G41, H75)
title: The Rise of Alternatives

abstract: Northvolt was one of Europe's most ambitious electric vehicle battery manufacturers and recyclers. The Group aimed to produce low-carbon and recycled lithium-ion batteries in the gigafactory Northvolt Ett located in Skellefteå, northern Sweden. Its rapid development and abrupt collapse in a seemingly favourable policy context provide a critical entry point into the political economy of Europe's decarbonisation and reindustrialisation agenda. Based on an interdisciplinary single-case study, this article reconstructs Northvolt's trajectory at multiple territorial and governance levels (across municipal, Swedish, Nordic, and European policy levels). It draws on a qualitative research framework combining documentary analysis, field visits in Sweden, and seventeen semi-structured interviews with a multi-level sample (workers, industrial actors, researchers, trade union representatives and policymakers). We show that Northvolt's arrival was embedded in a broader shift in transition governance, from sustainability-oriented goals towards geopolitical and supply-security concerns. Yet, this reframing lacked corresponding transformation of public intervention instruments, leaving limited public capacities for strategic coordination and crisis response. This article analyses how this policy architecture helped Northvolt to build financial credibility, but simultaneously failed to address the project's systemic vulnerabilities. Two potential drivers of the failure at Northvolt Ett are examined in depth: offtake-related constraints and operational misalignments. Overall, the article brings an empirical analysis of the collapse of a European battery champion to the literature on the political economy of the energy transition.
title: The rise and fall of Northvolt: From sustainability to battery geopolitics and industrial failure in the European Nordics

abstract: Using data on Chinese A-share listed firms from 2005 to 2018, this study examines how a distrustful local environment measured by firms able but unwilling to honor court orders shapes supply chain geography. We find that when local trust conditions deteriorate, firms tend to reduce their reliance on local suppliers and customers. The effect is more pronounced among state-owned enterprises and in regions with less market segmentation or higher baseline trust. A reference-point salience explanation applies: where initial trust is high, increases in local dishonesty are more informative. The mechanisms include more off-site independent directors, a lower proportion of credit loans, greater interfirm capital occupation, and elevated operational risk. The erosion of informal institutions such as trust may prompt firms to sidestep local partners. This study extends the literature on determinants of supply chain structure by incorporating informal institutional factors, and contributes to the literature on economic consequences of distrust.

abstract: We examine whether lenders incorporate behavioral signals into consumer credit pricing. Exploiting regulatory credit card reforms that altered the information content of a sophisticated credit card behavior, we show that borrowers exhibiting less sophisticated credit card usage subsequently experienced significantly higher default and bankruptcy rates across multiple consumer lending products. Despite this predictive power, lenders did not price this signal ex ante. Instead, contract terms adjusted only after repayment deterioration became observable through traditional credit metrics. These findings reveal a timing gap between observing predictive behavioral information and incorporating it into pricing decisions.
title: Behavioral signals and credit pricing: Evidence from credit cards

abstract: We study how large language model (LLM) based recommendations affect evaluations of uncertainty. We elicit certainty equivalents for (i) lotteries that share the same reduced-form winning probability but vary in cognitive demands because they are compound, and (ii) an Ellsberg-style ambiguous lottery. Across all lottery types, valuations from participants who receive LLM-based recommendations before each valuation exhibit second-order stochastic dominance relative to valuations from participants who do not. Hence, LLM-based recommendations leave mean valuations unchanged but compress the distribution, reducing the incidence of extreme valuations. Consistent with this pattern, LLM-based recommendations reduce the intensity of risk, complexity, and ambiguity aversion, while leaving the fraction of participants classified as averse unchanged.
title: The impact of LLM-based recommendations on decisions under uncertainty

abstract: Teamwork is prevalent in many forms of production, but individual contributions to team output are often ambiguous. We use a large-scale online experiment with an interactive team task to investigate gender differences in claiming credit for contributions to teamwork with misaligned incentives: Team members have an incentive to exaggerate their contribution, but this harms the other team member. In this setting, we observe that men claim to have contributed more than equally contributing women. Using two further between-subject treatments, we find no evidence that gender differences in altruism or in overconfidence explain the observed gender claim-gap. Further, the gender gap is present only among high contributors, and we show that the gap is particularly pronounced for large claims, which has potentially important consequences for gender equity in labour market outcomes.
title: Borrowed plumes: the gender gap in claiming credit for teamwork

abstract: This paper examines whether the difference between equal-weighted (EW) market returns and value-weighted (VW) market returns can predict future realized volatility. Using Chinese market-level and sector-level data, the paper applies a heterogeneous autoregressive realized volatility (HAR-RV) model to test whether the market return difference contains incremental information for forecasting realized volatility. Both in-sample and out-of-sample results indicate that the return difference provides predictive information beyond the benchmark model. The predictive power mainly comes from periods in which EW returns underperform VW returns. After controlling for the corresponding negative return in each regression, the return difference retains some predictive power at the aggregate level and in selected sectors. Overall, the difference between EW and VW returns can serve as an internal market risk-state indicator for volatility forecasting.

abstract: Could anti-redistributive sentiment have long-run roots in Red Scare-era propaganda? In the 1930s and 40s, the media mogul William Randolph Hearst espoused vehement anti-communist rhetoric in his newspapers. Fears of socialism went head-to-head with FDR’s New Deal, the first wide-scale federal spending program. Using variation in newspaper penetration across U.S. counties, I show that an increase of 10 percentage points in Hearst circulation per capita decreased support for FDR by 2.1 percentage points. I also show evidence that these effects are long run, decreasing support for public healthcare and welfare programs through the late twentieth century.
title: The Effect of Red Scare Propaganda on U.S. Public Opinion: Evidence from the Newspapers of William Randolph Hearst

abstract: We describe the small amount of wage information in online job posts in the U.S. and how te information that is available is systematically correlated with occupation wages, firms wages, and local labor market tightness. Only 14% of posts contain any information, and 75% of all posts are accounted for by firms with pay information in less than 5% of their posts. More than half of posts with pay information list a range that, on average, is wide, spanning 28% of the midpoint (e.g. $21-28/hr or $32,000-$42,000/yr). The lack of information is not ‘missing at random’. First, postings for high wage occupations and at high wage firms are less likely to provide any wage information, more likely to use ranges when they do, and wider ranges at that. Second, average wages in job postings are higher than workers’ wages in CPS and OES data, especially at the bottom of the wage distribution, by around 40 percent. In low wage salaried positions this jumps to 80 percent. Our results are exemplified by the top 20 posting private, which are representative of the U.S. economy, but have wage information in less than 2% of their posts, while the top 20 firms with wage information are unrepresentative of the U.S. economy.
title: Online job posts contain very little wage information

abstract: We introduce Government Bond Market Distress Index (GMDI), a new index that tracks distress in the secondary market for government bonds. It combines the three essential dimensions: returns, volatility, and liquidity. We demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing market distress within the context of lira-denominated government bond market in Türkiye. We find that GMDI is negatively associated with economic outcomes measured by a number of real output and business sentiment indicators. The index is flexible enough to be adapted to a wide range of countries and hence could be used to quantify local government bond market distress as an alternative to sovereign credit default spreads.
title: Introducing a new Government bond market distress index: The case of Türkiye

abstract: Whether economic incentives matter for crime is studied in a novel way, from expensive precious metal thefts by thieves stealing catalytic converters from cars. Sharp and sizable variations in the prices of precious metals embedded in converters are combined with newly assembled U.S. crime data. Precipitously fast increases in precious metal prices generated a sizeable rise in auto-part thefts, while subsequent price declines and policy responses quickly reversed this pattern. The resulting boom-and-bust dynamics provide clean evidence that prices affect crime, and for these crimes that local resale infrastructure and target availability shape both the magnitude of this effect and the effectiveness of policy response.
title: Crime and Prices:Thefts of expensive precious metals from cars

abstract: To strengthen land resource governance, China has established a satellite-ground integrated land use law enforcement (LULE) system, in which remote sensing imagery is used to identify potential anomalies and on-site photographs provide essential evidence for subsequent administrative inspection. However, the large-scale interpretation of on-site photographs remains highly dependent on manual inspection, resulting in substantial administrative workloads, potential inconsistency in enforcement judgments, and limited transparency in evidence interpretation. To address these challenges, the study proposes an intelligent evidence interpretation framework based on deep neural networks and a clue knowledge graph to support on-site photograph inspection in LULE. The framework establishes a hierarchical evidence-processing workflow, in which a cross-scale attention-convolution fusion (CAF) model performs preliminary scene interpretation, a positional prior-constrained object detection (PPOD) method extracts enforcement-related visual clues, and a clue knowledge graph connects these observations with land-use compliance rules for traceable reasoning. Experimental results on 102,519 real-world on-site photographs covering eight LULE scenarios in Guangdong Province demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially improves the reliability of compliance-related evidence interpretation compared with conventional scene interpretation approaches, while providing traceable evidence chains for administrative review. The proposed framework provides an intelligent evidence-processing approach that supports more efficient, consistent, transparent, and evidence-based land-use law enforcement practices.

abstract: For a broad class of principal-agent problems, and for “almost all” specifications of the distribution of the agent’s type, any two optimal mechanisms are equivalent: conditional on each type of the agent, neither the principal nor the agent cares which mechanism is in force. Nearly-optimal mechanisms are nearly equivalent. This provides substantial reassurance about numerical analysis of mechanisms in applied work, and has important theoretical implications as well. The model allows for both adverse selection and moral hazard. The substantive assumptions are that the set of types is finite, and a separability assumption on the agent’s utility.
title: Equivalence and Near-Equivalence of Solutions to Principal-Agent Problems

abstract: Social media has lowered the barriers to political communication, allowing politicians to reach large audiences without relying on traditional media. Yet easier access does not imply an equal distribution of attention. This column examines this distinction by linking daily data on Twitter likes and campaign contributions for US Members of Congress in 2019–2020. The market for attention is winner-takes-all: returns become substantial only when politicians go viral, and a handful of stars capture a disproportionate share of the gains. Social media has combined unusually broad access to political communication with a highly unequal distribution of attention – and of the financial returns associated with it.
authors: Johannes Böken, Mirko Draca, Nicola Mastrorocco, Arianna Ornaghi
title: The returns to viral media

abstract: Official development assistance fell by 23% in 2025, the largest drop on record. Aid disbursements have tended to coincide with deposits in offshore banks. This column argues that once the Panama Papers raised the cost of offshore banking, part of that diversion migrated to cryptocurrency. Linking World Bank disbursements to blockchain forensics, it finds sharp, short-lived surges of anonymous crypto activity on tax-haven exchanges in the month aid arrives, implying leakage of two to six cents per aid dollar. The public ledgers that carry diverted funds also make them detectable, which argues for supervision timed to the moment the money lands.
authors: Sumit Agarwal, Peiyi Jin, Eswar Prasad, Daniel Rabetti
title: Crypto capture of foreign aid

abstract: Protected areas are increasingly expected to secure both biodiversity and Indigenous territorial rights, but that dual mandate breaks down where the rights-holders are peoples living in isolation, who cannot be consulted, cannot sit on a management council and cannot consent to any use of their territory. In Brazil, many live in Conservation Units (CUs) rather than in regularized Indigenous Lands (ILs). While both are recognized as protected areas (PAs), only ILs are expressly designated to secure Indigenous territorial rights. Through spatial analysis of Indigenous Peoples in Isolation (IPI) records, CUs, and ILs, combined with a systematic review of CU management plans, this article demonstrates that current PA management policy is structurally unprepared to address the territorial protection demands of isolated Indigenous groups. Of the 124 IPI records analyzed, 22 (17.7%) are located exclusively within CUs, 29 (23.3%) are in areas where CUs and ILs overlap, 65 are exclusively in ILs, and eight are outside any protected area. Fifty CUs of different categories and levels of institutional governance are associated with at least one IPI record. Of these, 23 are fully protected (IUCN Categories Ia and II), and 27 are for sustainable use (IUCN Categories IV, V, and VI). Only five of the 50 CUs have specific territorial policies for IPI. These figures reveal a governance gap that existing PA management policy has systematically failed to address: the majority of CUs with IPI presence operate without any formal zoning or protocol for these populations. Addressing this gap requires stronger inter-institutional coordination between FUNAI and ICMBio, IPI-specific governance measures in CU management plans, and formal protocols to ensure territorial protection while respecting Indigenous peoples' decision to remain in isolation. Equivalent overlaps between conservation-designated areas and peoples in isolation occur in Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, so the mismatch identified here is structural to any country operating two territorial protection systems under two different mandates.
title: Indigenous peoples in isolation inside protected areas: Mandate mismatch and inter-institutional coordination gaps in the Brazilian Amazon

abstract: Using modifications of Lindeberg’s interpolation technique, I propose a new identification-robust test for the structural parameter in a heteroskedastic instrumental variables model. My analysis accommodates both scenarios where the number of instruments is much larger than the sample size and scenarios with few instruments, thus making the test broadly applicable. The proposed test statistic has a limiting chi-squared distribution so long as an auxiliary parameter can be consistently estimated. This is possible with standard methods when the number of instruments is small or using machine learning methods when the intruments are high-dimensional. To improve power, a simple combination with the sup-score statistic is proposed. The flexibility of my asymptotic approach allows for higher quality first-stage estimators to be used in the construction of the test statistic which provides noticeable power improvements over existing tests, both in Monte Carlo simulations calibrated to empirical data and in an application to the returns to education. Motivated by empirical practice, I also point out that first-stage F-statistics calculated on LASSO-selected variables may be misleading indicators of identification strength.
title: An identification-and dimensionality-robust test for instrumental variables models
